papers.title_in_file: Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Quantum Machine Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, related work, contributions, Section 3 (time dependence), Section 4 theory statements (Theorem 2), Sections 5.2 to 5.4 (results, limitations), Section 6 conclusion. Appendix proofs not read.
papers.what_it_is: A TMLR paper that adapts Adaptive Conformal Inference to quantum conformal prediction (AQCP) to handle time-varying hardware noise, tested on IBM ibm_sherbrooke shot data.

assertions.value: The authors introduce Adaptive Quantum Conformal Prediction (AQCP) and state that it provides asymptotic average coverage guarantees under arbitrary hardware noise conditions.
quotes: We introduce Adaptive Quantum Conformal Prediction (AQCP), an algorithm which provides asymptotic average coverage guarantees under arbitrary hardware noise conditions.
These guarantees do not depend on exchangeability.
assertions.certainty_reason: Asymptotic guarantee inherited from Gibbs and Candes adaptive conformal inference, stated in Section 4, p.9; finite-sample Theorem 2 adapted with proof in Appendix C.1 (not read).
assertions.reader_inference: The guarantee is asymptotic in the number of test points, so it says nothing about any short window.

assertions.value: The authors report that empirical studies on an IBM quantum processor show AQCP achieves the target coverage level and is more stable than quantum conformal prediction.
quotes: Empirical studies on an IBM quantum processor demonstrate that AQCP achieves the target coverage level and exhibits greater stability than quantum conformal prediction.
Confidently attributing the greater deviation of QCP from the target coverage level to non-stationary noise would require further experimentation
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one set of hardware runs; the authors themselves say the attribution to non-stationary noise needs further experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: The stability gain is shown, but its cause is not isolated by the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that without the assumption of stationary noise, the standard conformal guarantee cannot be obtained, because the time-dependent quantum shots make the conformity scores not necessarily exchangeable.
quotes: without making the assumption of stationary noise, we cannot obtain guarantees in the form given in Theorem 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3 states the condition under which the standard quantum conformal guarantee holds.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hardware evaluation covers runs from a single day, so it does not fully characterise longer-term drift, and that AQCP is inherently sequential and so is not directly applicable in batch prediction settings.
quotes: hardware runs collected over a single day and therefore does not fully characterise longer-term drift or more structured perturbations
we note that AQCP is inherently sequential: it updates the miscoverage level using observed outcomes and thus requires that each test response be revealed before the next prediction is made.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.4 Limitations and Future Work, p.17.

papers.title_in_file: Performance Guarantees for Quantum Neural Estimation of Entropies
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction and summary of contributions, literature review, Section 2.3 footnote, Section 6 concluding remarks. Theorem statements and proofs (Sections 3 to 5, appendices) not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper (Quantum, 2026) giving non-asymptotic error bounds and copy-complexity bounds for quantum neural estimators of measured relative entropies.

assertions.value: The authors state that this work initiates the study of formal guarantees for quantum neural estimators of measured relative entropies in the form of non-asymptotic error risk bounds, and that the error is sub-Gaussian and sharply concentrates about the ground truth value.
quotes: This work initiates the study of formal guarantees for QNEs of measured
We further establish exponential tail bounds showing that the error is sub-Gaussian and thus sharply concentrates about the ground truth value.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 and Theorem 5, Section 3 (pp.11 to 16), proofs in Section 5; theorem statements and proofs not read in full by this reader.

assertions.value: The authors state the bounds assume the neural net and quantum circuit are sufficiently expressive with bounded statistical complexity, and that the quantum neural estimator has a worst case copy complexity that scales exponentially in the number of qudits, improving to polynomial for permutation invariant states.
quotes: Assuming that the neural net and quantum circuit are sufficiently expressive and have bounded statistical complexity

although the quantum neural estimator has a worst case copy complexity that scales exponentially in the number of qudits, this improves to polynomial when the underlying states are permutation invariant.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.1 and Section 6 state the conditions and the worst case scaling of the results.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optimization error, including the investigation of barren plateaus and local optima, was neglected in the analysis.
quotes: One such issue pertains to the quantification of the optimization error and an analysis of optimization dynamics such as the investigation of barren plateaus and local optima, which was neglected here.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6 concluding remarks, p.28.
assertions.reader_inference: The guarantees cover statistical error only; training failure is outside them.

papers.title_in_file: End-to-End Speedup for Quantum Simulation-Based Optimization in Power Grid Management
papers.version_note: The file name carries the v1 title (Scaling Quantum Simulation-Based Optimization, Demonstrating ...); the file is arXiv 2505.16444v2 titled End-to-End Speedup for Quantum Simulation-Based Optimization in Power Grid Management. Same arXiv id, so the record matches.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Sections V (end of) to VII (discussion, conclusion). Methods and dataset sections only skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of a QAOA-based quantum simulation-based optimization solver for the unit commitment problem, run by classical simulation of the quantum circuit and compared with simulated annealing.

assertions.value: The authors report that 16 QAOA layers suffice to outperform a strong classical baseline for problems involving up to 14 qubits in scenarios of high load, and that QAOA performs on par otherwise.
quotes: We show that 16 QAOA layers suffice to outperform a strong classical baseline for problems involving up to 14 qubits in scenarios of high load and perform on par otherwise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one numerical study on simulated circuits and random instances.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is on simulated circuits of at most 14 qubits and an NP-hard problem, so the speedup is in the simulation sub-routine scaling, not a hardware result.

assertions.value: The authors state the experiments used randomly generated power grid instances and a classical simulation of the quantum circuit that bypasses the ancillary qubit requirements of the original algorithm.
quotes: The numerical experiments were conducted using randomly generated power grid instances of varying sizes and loads that adhere to the physical properties of real world power grids.
allowing for large-scale experiments.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantum hardware run is reported in what this reader saw.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QAOA was not able to reach near-optimal solution quality in most cases, and attribute this to the parameter optimization method.
quotes: A noteworthy detail from our analysis is that the QAOA was not able to reach near-optimal solution quality in most cases.
Future work should definitely conduct a broader hyperparameter search and expand the evaluation to larger problem instances.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VII conclusion, p.8.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the QAOA's lack of near-optimal approximation ratios stems only from insufficient or unsuitable parameter optimization.
quotes: we conclude that this only stems from insufficient and/or unsuitable parameter optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author conclusion; the conclusion section says it is likely and not tested.

papers.title_in_file: On Quantum Perceptron Learning via Quantum Search
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Section 1 introduction and contributions, Section 5.2 practical limitations, Section 6 conclusion. Algorithm constructions, proofs and appendices not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that corrects a complexity assumption in the quantum version space perceptron and proposes two quantum-enhanced cutting-plane perceptron algorithms with query complexity analyses.

assertions.value: The authors show that the query complexity of the quantum version space perceptron algorithm is dimension-dependent, correcting a flawed complexity assumption in the earlier work.
quotes: by identifying and correcting a flawed complexity assumption.
We show that the query complexity of the algorithm is dimensiondependent, which has significant implications for its behaviour in high-dimensional regimes under worst-case scenarios.
assertions.certainty_reason: Abstract and Section 1.1 statement of a result; the proof and the simulation check were not read by this reader.

assertions.value: The authors state that their two quantum-enhanced cutting-plane algorithms have improved complexity bounds under an idealised implementation framework and noise-free quantum computational models.
quotes: Our results establish improved complexity bounds under an idealised implementation framework and noise-free quantum computational models
assertions.certainty_reason: Abstract statement; theorems not read by this reader.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reported speedups characterise the asymptotic potential of quantum perceptron models under an idealised setup, and are not guarantees of real-time performance.
quotes: the reported speedups should be viewed as characterising the asymptotic potential of quantum perceptron models under idealised setup
defer simulations, small-scale tests, and fault-tolerant schemes to future work
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1.1 states the scope of the results.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results should be viewed as conceptual, asymptotic improvements rather than immediately realisable practical speedups on either NISQ or fault-tolerant quantum platforms.
quotes: Taken together, these observations suggest that our results should be viewed as conceptual, asymptotic improvements, rather than immediately realisable practical speedups on either NISQ or fault-tolerant quantum platforms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5.2 practical limitations, p.24.

papers.title_in_file: Distributed and Secure Kernel-Based Quantum Machine Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction and contributions, Section 6.2 and 6.3 protocol and security, Section 7 experimental evaluation text, Section 8 conclusion. Appendix proofs and Table 1 values not read.
papers.what_it_is: A paper proposing quantum feature maps for polynomial, RBF and Laplacian kernels and a teleportation-based architecture for secure distributed kernel computation, validated on a simulator for the linear kernel.

assertions.value: The authors state that they introduce quantum feature maps for the polynomial, Radial Basis Function (RBF), and Laplacian kernels and theoretically prove the correctness of these feature maps.
quotes: We introduce quantum feature maps for the polynomial, Radial Basis Function (RBF), and Laplacian kernels and theoretically prove the correctness of these feature maps.
assertions.certainty_reason: Contribution statement; the proofs (appendix) were not read by this reader.

assertions.value: The authors report that, on a simulator, their approach achieves performance comparable to centralized classical and quantum methods, and they report no timings because the experiments ran on a simulator.
quotes: Our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed approach ensures data security and achieves performance comparable to centralized classical and quantum methods.
Note that we do not report any timings since the experiments are run on a simulator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from simulator runs on three public datasets; accuracy table not read.

assertions.value: The authors state that only the linear kernel was tested, because of the simulator limits and lack of access to a real quantum computer, so the other kernels were not tested.
quotes: Due to the limitations of the simulator and our lack of access to a real quantum computer, we were unable to test other kernels at this stage.
Our experiments focused on computing the linear kernel.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 1 contribution 3 and Section 7, pp.2 and 12.

assertions.value: The authors state the security analysis assumes semi-honest clients and server, that malicious participants can affect the accuracy of the model, and that handling actively malicious entities is future work.
quotes: In our proposed adversarial model, clients, including Alice and Bob, as well as the server, are semi-honest.
However, malicious participants can affect the accuracy of the model.
In the future, our aim is to adapt our methodology to scenarios that involve actively malicious entities.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 6.3 adversarial model and Section 8 conclusion.

papers.title_in_file: Phase-Space Framework for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Optical Neural Networks
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section IV discussion (stability, initialisation, comparison), Section V conclusions. Model sections and appendices not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A simulation paper using the phase-space positive-P method to model large bosonic quantum reservoir neural networks for quantum state classification and feature prediction.

assertions.value: The authors report that the performance of a large quantum reservoir does not improve monotonously with the number of bosonic modes, and that reservoirs with five to seven nodes achieve optimal performance for the analysed tasks.
quotes: Our results show that the performance of a large quantum reservoir does not improve monotonously with the number of bosonic modes
We show that reservoirs with five to seven nodes achieve optimal performance for the analysed quantum machine learning tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from classical simulations of specific reservoirs and two tasks.
assertions.reader_inference: The optimum applies to the analysed tasks and Kerr nonlinearities only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the work presents an efficient computational framework based on the phase-space positive-P method for simulating bosonic neuromorphic systems, simulated on classical hardware, with no quantum hardware run.
quotes: This work presents an efficient computational framework based on the phase-space positive-P method for simulating bosonic neuromorphic systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states what the work does: a simulation framework.
assertions.reader_inference: The reader's note that no hardware run is reported rests on the paper describing only simulation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the positive-P method can become unstable in closed systems because of noise amplification, and that input initialisation may limit the class of quantum states that can be reliably injected into the reservoir.
assertions.anchor: Section IV A and B, pp.9 to 10
quotes: The positive-P method can become unstable in closed systems due to the effect of noise amplification
Consequently, input initialisation may limit the class of quantum states that can be reliably injected into the reservoir.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV A and B, pp.9 to 10.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum-inspired algorithm applied to extreme learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, the uniform-sampling experiment text (Section III), Section IV conclusion. Algorithm derivations not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: An empirical study applying the quantum-inspired (dequantized) low-rank SVD algorithm to extreme learning and comparing norm-based with uniform sampling.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum-inspired algorithm works an order of magnitude faster than the exact SVD when high-dimensional feature vectors are used.
quotes: We implement the algorithm and observe that it works order-of-magnitude faster than the exact SVD when we use high-dimensional feature vectors.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical runtime result from one implementation on the authors' datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a classical algorithm; the speedup is against exact classical SVD, not a quantum speedup.

assertions.value: The authors report that for random features generated by random neural networks, uniform sampling gives the same level of test accuracy as the norm-based sampling, because the matrix is uniform in this case.
quotes: we can replace the norm-based sampling in the quantum-inspired algorithm with uniform sampling to obtain the same level of test accuracy due to the uniformity of the matrix in this case.
Therefore, our concern that the Frobenius-norm sampling can be replaced by uniform sampling seems to be correct
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experiment on two datasets.
assertions.reader_inference: In the naive setting, the part of the algorithm that comes from the quantum algorithm (norm-based sampling) added nothing.

assertions.value: The authors state that their implementation of the mod-FKV algorithm is not optimized for speed.
quotes: our implementation of mod-FKV algorithm is not optimized for speed.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV conclusion, p.6.

papers.title_in_file: Geometric Quantum Physics Informed Neural Network
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section VII summary and outlook, expressibility method paragraph. Sections III to VI (constructions, benchmarks) not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A paper introducing symmetry-aware quantum physics-informed neural networks (GQPINNs) for PDEs, benchmarked against QPINN and classical PINN baselines.

assertions.value: The authors report that across their benchmarks, GQPINNs achieve lower mean absolute error than standard QPINNs while requiring substantially fewer trainable parameters.
quotes: Across these benchmarks, GQPINNs achieve improved solution accuracy, as quantified by lower mean absolute error, while requiring substantially fewer trainable parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from the authors' benchmarks on a few PDEs.

assertions.value: The authors state they benchmark GQPINNs against standard QPINNs and symmetry-adapted classical PINN baselines under matched training protocols across a representative set of linear and nonlinear PDEs.
quotes: We benchmark GQPINNs against standard QPINNs and symmetry-adapted classical PINN baselines under matched training protocols across a representative set of linear and nonlinear PDEs.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the benchmark setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that K4GQPINN is competitive with the corresponding symmetry-invariant classical PINN but does not provide a consistent improvement at comparable parameter counts.
quotes: K4GQPINN is competitive with the corresponding SI-PINN but does not provide a consistent improvement at comparable parameter counts
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one benchmark (2D Poisson).
assertions.reader_inference: Part of the gain over QPINN comes from symmetry, which a classical PINN can also use.

assertions.value: The authors state that their current approach enforces symmetry primarily at the level of the target solution, and that richer point symmetries such as translations and scalings are future work.
quotes: our current approach enforces symmetry primarily at the level of the target solution, for example rotational invariance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VII summary and outlook.
